title: In a Portrait
text:
When,

beneath the quadrangular heap

of fresh earth that must bury me,

and after

it has already rained a great deal,

when the grass advances toward oblivion,

still,

friend, my gaze of old,

crossing the sea, will come, without deception,

to

enfold you in a tender gesture,

like that of a poor grateful

dog.


Version by Amador Palacios
editorial_note: The translation preserves the posthumous gaze crossing the sea and the translator/version note.

title: The Lily
text:
To Raúl Rivero

I carry a fantastic, tremendous lily;

beautiful outside and inside bad.

It frightens me with its thirst. I give it, I

sell it,

I gift it to anyone who passes.


Let it go grow; tall, upright,

in the hardest earth of another

shoulder.

To me it gives loose pain in the chest,

solitary and standing like

rubble.


Its impoverished reflection bothers me,

its not wanting to become oblivion,


its intolerable and ashen silk.


Take it away from me! Quickly... I ask it.

Make a blind heart,

abolished,

of this lily that at last settles in me!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the dedication and the lily as beautiful, bad, and painfully lodged.

title: The Tongue Above All, Affectionate...
text:
The tongue above all, affectionate,

rough and courtly in greeting.


The paws for embracing, with what care,

or for begging affection, or harm, from the one who tames it.


The caress with claws, the chest belly-up

to show the captive heart.


The whole skin surrendered, the hoarse voice

romping in its cage of fangs,

and the enormous eyes, of seaweed, smiling

at the immediate death

to which it was sentenced.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the tamed animal's affectionate menace and death-sentenced gaze.

title: Birds for Yvonne
text:
Your body in what joy of fluttering,

what nearness of trills, oh agitated

passion of you, inspired turtledove,

of blue and feather in clear blue! (Uccello)


Bird. Go out. Write on the ground

the joy of your enamored cage.

Let the sword of a hawk

brandished for the duel be a smiling perch.


I, your parted foliage. Permanent

tree where your destiny resounds,

will read your trajectory. One guesses


so well what is awaited... Of the oblique

path, what do you care, oh different

blackbird of light, if you come to the holm oak!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the bird imagery, Uccello aside, and the beloved's flight toward the tree.

title: I Cry Out to Your Livid Belly of Wind...
text:
I cry out to your livid belly of wind,

to the narrow heart of your roosters,

to their red whips, to the rays

that riddle your hollow firmament.


I seek the edge of unfolding,

to steal myself as fruit from my normal stems,

to free myself in your acid horses

and to anoint your towers with my advent.


If you came with me to the undulating

high hill of being, where living blood

turns into the symbol of ice...


But who will be able to stop the dawn,

already lifting the shell of its route,

its raptors of light over your flight.




1951
editorial_note: The translation keeps Barral's turbulent apostrophe and the dawn's raptors of light.

title: Skinny-Dipping
text:
To have desired it vividly and see them

tread the water that the moon muddies,

and to stand watching them; the white bodies

breaking the shadow of the shining metal

—universal nakedness, nakedness unto death—

and remain undecided, standing, in the dark,

like an old sailor suspecting a time

suddenly adventurous, and then,

forgetting the remains of the sad supper

with guitar and saliva-wet bottle necks,

enter with the charge of a whole animal,

called by the water or by the bodies.


It runs to the castrating edge of cold,

water like swords.

The statues

soften among laughter, in the foam.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the voyeuristic hesitation, animal plunge, and sword-cold water.

title: Butterfly, Flower of Air...
text:
Butterfly, flower of air,

combs the area of the rose.

Everything is like that, butterfly,

when one lives in the air.

And the hours of air are

those of the voices that fly.

Only in the voices that fly

does the heart carry wings.

Carry them away from here, for they are

the only voices that fly.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the airy circularity of butterfly, rose, voice, and heart.

title: She Is the Festival of Lines...
text:
She is the festival of lines

and of dreaming roses

and the Apollonian diadems

among the flower of dawns.

Troop of fisher gods...

Pindar sings, Aspasia dictates.

And a trampling of visions

in the sighs of magic...

Solemnity of colonnade.

And in the platinum jaws

of the tripod, lifts its efforts

the lividity of aromas,

like a gust of verses

in an enchantment of doves...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the classical cascade of lines, roses, Pindar, Aspasia, and doves.
